title: Jet lag and the first days at a new ground
summary: How long jet lag lasts, how light, sleep and a spare day can help, and how to start shooting at a new ground after a long flight.

body.html: Jet lag happens when your body clock is still on home time after a fast trip across at least three time zones. Sleep, appetite, mood and alertness are out of step with local time until the clock catches up.

Tiredness from the journey itself is a different thing. A long trip by car, train or plane brings stiff muscles, short sleep and dry air, even with no time difference. It often eases after rest, while jet lag lasts until the body clock has adjusted.

A common rough guide to how long jet lag lasts: about one day per time zone after flying east, and about half a day per time zone after flying west. The more time zones you cross, the stronger the symptoms tend to be. People differ, so treat these numbers as an estimate.

Many people find flying east harder than flying west. After a flight east you have to fall asleep earlier than your body is used to, and that is harder than going to bed later. Early risers often adapt to flights east more easily, and night owls to flights west.

Light is the main signal that sets the body clock. After a flight a few time zones east (up to about 8), get daylight in the morning and keep the evening dim. After flying west, do the opposite: avoid bright morning light and get light in the late afternoon and evening. After a longer flight east, it may work better to move the body clock later instead of earlier, and light at the wrong hours can shift it the wrong way. So before such a trip, you can ask a sports doctor for a plan.

Before a flight about two time zones east, you can start adjusting at home. For 2–3 days before you leave, go to bed and get up 30–60 minutes earlier, and go out into bright light soon after waking. Before longer flights east, it is better to ask a sports doctor for a plan.
From the first day, live on local time: eat, sleep and plan the day by it, and spend time in daylight. A short nap early in the day can help; keep it short, so that night sleep does not suffer.
Protect your sleep: a cool, dark and quiet room, no late heavy dinners, and no alcohol on the evening before a shooting day. More in Competition day: sleep, coffee, water and food.

Coffee in the local morning can help you feel more awake, but keep to your usual amount and do not add an extra dose on a shooting day. For shooters, research sees little benefit in caffeine, and large doses can make your hands less steady. Avoid coffee from the late afternoon, so that it does not spoil your sleep.

Some sports doctors use melatonin — a substance the body makes in the evening and at night, also sold as tablets — to help the body clock adjust. As with the other methods in this lesson, research in athletes is limited. Ask a doctor before you try it: the time of day you take it matters, and the rules for selling it differ between countries. Supplements can contain banned substances: see Medicines and anti-doping: beta-blockers, TUE, supplements. If you have a health condition or take medicines, talk to a doctor before a long trip.

After a long flight east, plan a spare day before shooting for score. Use it for an easy session, not hard training: sports doctors suggest a light or medium workload on the first day, nothing heavy. This advice comes from other sports; it probably applies to clay shooting too.

A new ground needs getting used to as well. The backgrounds (what you see behind the target — sky, trees, a hillside), the light and the target colours differ from your home ground. You can try starting with a few easy targets, just to see how they look against the new background. Where you may practise before a competition depends on the discipline: Planning the trip.
Check your lens tint — the colour of your shooting-glasses lenses — on each new layout: a tint that works on one stand may not work on the next. More in Shooting glasses and lens colours.

If you organise a tour, put a spare day into the programme after long flights east, before any shooting for score. Make the first session easy, give the timetable in the venue's time zone with the zone labelled, and avoid late dinners or alcohol events before shooting days.

notes.html: A useful habit on a tour: on the first day, run a short lens and background check, and let the group note which tint worked on which stand.

key_points.html: How long it lasts, roughly: about one day per time zone after flying east, and about half a day per time zone after flying west.
After a flight a few time zones east (up to about 8): daylight in the morning, dim evenings; after flying west, the opposite.
After the journey: local time from the first day, water and an easy first session.
Plan a spare day before shooting for score after a long flight east.
On a new ground, you can start with a few easy targets; check your lens tint.

did_you_know.html: Your phone usually switches to local time by itself, but a watch or the clock in your own car may not. Check them after landing, because shooting times are given in local time.

quiz.q: After a flight a few time zones east (up to about 8), which light pattern helps the body clock adjust?

options.text: Bright light in the evening and dark mornings
Daylight in the morning and a dim evening
A dark room for the whole first day

quiz.explain: After such a flight the body clock has to move earlier, and morning light helps it do that. For very long flights east, a doctor may suggest a different plan.

quiz.q: What is a common rough guide for jet lag after flying east?

options.text: About one hour in total, whatever the distance
About one week, whatever the distance
About one day per time zone crossed

quiz.explain: A common rough guide: jet lag lasts about a day per time zone after flying east and about half a day per time zone after flying west.

quiz.q: What is a sensible first session at a new ground?

options.text: A few easy targets to see the new background
A full competition round, to test yourself
No shooting at all until the jet lag has gone

quiz.explain: Easy targets first let you see how targets look against the new background and light.
